blocks.text: Jenny’s editor sent her back to the waterfront for a different story. The Blackwell Foundation wanted to invest in the lakefront now that people were returning to the clearer water.

blocks.alt: Claude Blackwell announces his lakefront investment plans beside his wife Eleanor while Jenny takes notes.
blocks.text: Claude Blackwell, a wealthy philanthropist with swept-back gray hair and a dark suit, stood at the podium. Beside him was his wife, Eleanor Blackwell, her silver curls neatly arranged above tinted sunglasses. Sunlight flashed on the lenses as she turned toward the crowd while Claude unfolded his lakefront plans.

One of the plans showed the path from Public Square toward the water. Another newspaper clipping described the proposed Tower City redevelopment around the old Union Terminal. Claude laid it beside his own drawings. “People should be able to enjoy the shore, too.”
Claude unfolded plans for repaired paths and new waterfront businesses. He pointed out the damaged railing first. “Shops can wait. Nobody should have to risk a broken leg to reach the water.”
Jenny asked what had made the lake so clear in the first place. Eleanor answered before Claude could.
“Dr. Daniel Orkleson,” she said. “His invention has done remarkable work. Cleveland ought to give him credit.”

Jenny wrote down the claim. She had seen Daniel collecting light at the shore, but he had supplied no test results. Claude returned to the plans, pointing out where the damaged path needed attention before it could reopen.

blocks.alt: Claude shows Jenny his lakefront investment plan while a crew repairs a damaged railing.
blocks.text: Later that day, Claude showed Jenny the damaged railing with a repair crew beside him. He held the plan against the wind and listened as a worker explained what needed replacing. Whatever had cleared the water, he wanted the shore safe enough for people to use.
Jenny’s report described the investment plans and attributed the cleanup claim to Eleanor. She included that Orkleson had yet to provide the test results she had requested.

Billy read the report the next morning. Eleanor was his aunt. Seeing her give Daniel credit without evidence made him fold the paper sharply enough to crease her photograph. That afternoon, he went to the Blackwells’ home.

blocks.alt: Billy visits his aunt Eleanor and Claude at their home, bringing the newspaper report beside Claude’s lakefront plans.
blocks.text: Claude welcomed Billy and spread the lakefront plan across the sitting-room table. Eleanor offered tea. Billy kept the newspaper in his hands.
“Aunt Eleanor, why did you say Daniel cleaned the lake?”
She glanced at the paper. “Because he says he did. I have no reason to doubt him.”
“I saw the machine,” Billy said. “Its meter moved. Its case filled with light. Daniel wouldn’t tell us what it collected. None of that proves he cleaned the lake.”
“William, you’ve disliked Daniel for years,” Eleanor said. “You can hardly expect me to take that as evidence against him.”
“Then ask him for the test results. I’m asking for proof, not asking you to take my word.”
Eleanor set down her cup. “I see no reason to question him further. Leave him alone.”

“Has he published his results?” Claude asked. “Not that I’ve seen,” Billy said. Claude folded his plan. “Then I’ll ask for them. We can repair a railing without pretending we know who cleared the water.”
Billy opened his notebook. Eleanor rose to refill the teapot. “Will you stay for lunch, William?”
Billy declined the invitation and took his newspaper home. He still intended to ask Daniel for the results.
